Patient demographics:
  age: 62
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Psychiatrist
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 47

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Media / News: Related news, Auditory (Language Confusion): Incomprehensible chatter, Authority Figures: People in uniform
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Going Out: Going out, Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Redirection: I think of something else
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture, Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down, No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences

Vignette:
Dr. Mateo Rojas presents as a composed, articulate man of sixty-two, his office a testament to a long and distinguished career in psychiatry. Books line the walls, and his desk is impeccably organized, projecting an aura of control and erudition that has become his primary defense. Yet, for nearly forty years, since he was a young medical student in his home country, Mateo has been living with the unhealed wounds of a past that refuses to stay buried. The event itself returns not as a coherent story but in brutal, sensory fragments. There are moments of searing clarity: the rough, damp texture of the blindfold against his eyelids, the metallic taste of fear in his mouth, the precise cadence of a particular officer's bootsteps on the concrete floor. But other parts are a complete blank, a void of time he cannot account for, which is perhaps even more terrifying. What remains most vivid is the sound—a cacophony of overlapping, angry voices speaking in a dialect he couldn't fully parse, a wall of incomprehensible chatter that signaled his total loss of control.

This sensory echo haunts his daily life, turning the most mundane environments into potential threats. The hospital where he has worked for two decades has become a landscape of triggers. The sight of a security guard making his rounds in the corridor can instantly cause a cold dread to wash over him. Mateo will immediately drop his gaze, his mind racing to rehearse the exact words he will say to his next patient, a desperate attempt to anchor himself in his professional role and away from the image of a different kind of uniform. The hospital cafeteria is entirely off-limits. The blended sounds of conversations, the clatter of trays, the sheer volume of human noise merge into that same overwhelming, incomprehensible chatter from the cell. When he is inadvertently exposed, like walking past its open doors, a memory can ignite without warning. Suddenly, it is not the smell of disinfectant and stale coffee in the air, but of sweat and urine, and he is back in the suffocating darkness of the blindfold, the feeling so real he has to brace himself against a wall. In these moments, he forces his mind elsewhere, a trick he has perfected over the years. He will seize upon a complex diagnostic puzzle, a difficult case study, anything to redirect his focus until the sensory reliving subsides.

Over the decades, his world has shrunk. He was once an active member of the local Latin American cultural center, a place of vibrant music, food, and shared language. But he began to avoid it, then stopped going altogether. The crowds and the loud, overlapping conversations became unbearable. This withdrawal has cemented a profound and painful belief that he has lost his connection to his own community, a feeling of being an outsider looking in. He sees his culture now through the television, but even that is fraught with peril. A news report on political unrest, a headline about activists disappearing, or any story of state-sanctioned violence feels like a personal confirmation that the world is fundamentally unjust. The people who tortured him were never brought to justice, a fact that fuels a deep, simmering anger and a conviction that the institutions meant to protect people are designed to fail them. This belief has curdled into a quiet cynicism that shadows his interactions, even at work.

The effort of maintaining his professional facade while navigating this internal minefield has become exhausting. He feels a growing sense of hypocrisy, offering guidance and solace to patients while his own mind is a war zone. The decision to seek therapy was not precipitated by a single crisis but by a slow, crushing accumulation of loneliness. He is single, his social circle has withered from his avoidance, and the silence of his apartment at night has grown deafening. He came to the first session with a quiet desperation, admitting that the strategies he had used to survive were now simply keeping him from living. What he fears most is that truly confronting the memories will shatter the fragile control he has clung to for forty years. What he hopes for, he said with a tremor in his voice, is to one day walk through a crowded room and hear only conversation, not a threat.
